prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The map places the camera wearer’s forearms, hands, and lower torso/legs in the near foreground, roughly 0.2–1.0 m from the camera; the reddish path lies below and ahead at about 1–2 m, while shrubs, rocks, and the pond edge are farther away, roughly 2–5 m. Across the five frames, the nearest body region shifts from the lower-left/centre toward the lower-right as the wearer turns or steps right, while the pond becomes more prominent at the upper right; no separate person is visible. The map makes the wearer’s body-to-ground separation and the foreground/background layering clearer than RGB, including occlusion of the path by the wearer’s torso and arms and cropping of the lower body by the frame edge. Absolute metre estimates are uncertain because the map is monocular, and several rocks, plants, shadows, and distant surfaces have similar dark values or blurred boundaries, so their relative depths are unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The map isolates one person—the camera wearer’s visible arms and body—in the lower foreground, with the mask partly cut off by the bottom edge and changing from left/centre in frame 1 to mostly centre-right by frame 5; it provides no evidence of another person or of anyone looking toward the wearer. Several small shrubs above and ahead are segmented and labelled “broccoli,” generally about 1–4 m from the wearer and separated from the body by the path, while one tiny region near the right hand in frame 3 is labelled “cell phone.” The masks make object extent, left/right ordering, partial visibility, and occlusion clearer than RGB: the wearer’s body covers part of the path, and the arms project upward into the scene, with nearby items around the hands plausibly within arm’s reach. The labels are unreliable—the “broccoli” regions appear to be ornamental shrubs, the possible phone mask is extremely small, and most rocks, path, pond, railing/cable, and vegetation receive no masks—so distances, object identity, facing direction, and contact cannot be recovered reliably from this map alone.
descriptions.pose: The pose map detects only magenta hand skeletons, with no yellow body skeleton and no skeleton belonging to another person; the detected hands correspond to the camera wearer’s hands roughly 0.3–0.8 m from the camera and are partly constrained by the image edges and self-occlusion. The hand detections move from far left in frame 1 to lower-left in frame 2, split around centre in frame 3, appear centre-right in frame 4, and end farther right in frame 5, supporting a rightward turn or change in arm position across time. Compared with RGB, the map makes the changing hand locations and rough finger/hand orientation easier to track against clutter, but it does not encode scene layout, depth, gaze, or whether objects are actually grasped. The tiny, fragmented skeletons are unreliable for exact joint positions, arm reach, facing direction, and inter-object distance, especially where hands overlap pale objects or are partly occluded.
